speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The trade conflict between the US and China and, indeed, with other trading partners, such as the European Union (EU), taking reciprocal measures in response to the US’ tariffs, will have global consequences.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Not only will it inhibit global trade and global growth, there will also be disruptions to supply chains impacting businesses, jobs and consumers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our economic agencies are closely monitoring the impact on Singapore which will be transmitted at three levels.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, impact from higher generalised tariffs that are applicable to the majority of countries, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is what we call the direct impact.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, the indirect impact arising from disruptions to global supply chains due to the tariffs imposed by the US and China directed at each other.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And third, the consequences of a broad-based slowdown in global trade flows if escalation of the trade conflict among the US, China and other trading partners spills over to business sentiment and other factors of growth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, tariffs directly applicable to Singapore affect a relatively small set of products.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These are essentially US tariffs applied globally on solar cells and modules, washing machines, steel and aluminium.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While this is relatively modest, specific Singapore-based companies in the general manufacturing and electronics sectors that export such products to the US will become less competitive compared to manufacturers in the US when the tariffs are added on.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our agencies are in contact with impacted companies to facilitate applications for product exclusion and to explore alternative markets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, there will be indirect impact from tariffs that are not targeted at Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members will have read about the US and China's imposition of tariffs on each other.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Tariffs applied to products worth US$34 billion from each country have kicked in, with more on the way.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With the EU, Mexico and Canada also imposing retaliatory tariffs on the US for the tariffs on steel and aluminium, there is a significant risk of widening disruption to global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While these tariffs do not directly affect our exports, they would have spillover impact due to our role in the global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, Singapore companies that produce intermediate goods used as inputs in the production of China’s exports to the US may see softer demand for their goods.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The net impact on the Singapore economy and our workers is less easily quantified, given the fluidity of the US and China’s tit-for-tat responses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The complexity of global value chains is also such that amidst disruptions, there will be potential for firms to mitigate some of the impact by redirecting exports of intermediate goods to other markets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In addition, traders in China which find imports from the US less competitive because of the tariffs may also source more from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) region.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our modelling indicates that based on the tariffs on product lines that have been announced, the net impact is likely to be modest.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, this assumes no further escalation in trade tensions between the US and China.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the meantime, our economic agencies are working closely with companies to identify any disruptions promptly and restructure their supply chains where necessary.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, our greatest concern is the impact from an escalation of the trade conflict into a vicious cycle of tit-for-tat measures among major economies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In this scenario, the impact on global consumption and investment on top of the disruption to trade flows will significantly impact Singapore's open economy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Amidst these developments, there are strengths in the composition and features of our economy that serve us well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These include the strong trading networks and diversified sectors we have developed over the years, which will enable companies in Singapore to navigate the disruptions and seek out new opportunities and alternative suppliers and demand markets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our agencies will continue to facilitate this process and provide support where needed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Thanaletchimi and Mr Henry Kwek have also asked about whether the norm of free trade agreements and the multilateral trading system of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) will change.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Indeed, the commitment to free and open trade has come under pressure, with greater protectionist instincts and the US’ unilateral measures to address what it has deemed unfair trade practices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Nevertheless, for the large majority of economies, the commitment to the WTO remains unchanged.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Numerous economies have made clear their stance on this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The US has stated its openness to bilateral trade agreements and has remained engaged in various international forums to share its views on improving the rules-based multilateral trading system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Singapore’s external linkages that have made us more resilient in facing uncertainties in the global economy are best safeguarded by a strong set of WTO rules and enforcement, and by our network of Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) which we will continue to expand and deepen.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are in good standing with all our trading partners, including the US and China, and have urged that ongoing trade disputes be resolved through negotiation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have also forged ahead with like-minded partners to continue paving the way for regional integration to bring about more opportunities and growth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our trading partners are also constantly looking for opportunities to improve trade links.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The EU and China, for example, which Mr Henry Kwek has asked about, are working to improve trade connectivity between Asia and Europe to increase economic opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have an FTA in place with China, and another that is pending with the EU.
